assumptions: The primary target operating system is Windows, as the developer is using Windows.
The application will have a Graphical User Interface (GUI) rather than being just a command-line tool.
The software is intended for personal desktop computers rather than server environments.
The initial release will target individual consumer users looking for a simple, fast cleanup utility.
candidates: File scanner for standard cache, temporary files, and log files.
Visual disk analyzer (e.g. Treemap/Sunburst chart) for large files and folders.
confirmed: The core purpose of the software is to scan and clean up disk space on a computer (磁盘清理/空间释放).
conflicts: Automated One-Click Cleanup vs. Granular Control: General users prefer a single button that 'just works' safely, while advanced users demand to see and approve every file before deletion.
Deep/Thorough Scan vs. Speed: Scanning deep directories or calculating file hashes (for duplicates) takes significant time, conflicting with the expectation of a lightweight and fast utility.

gaps.impact: High risk of bricking the user's OS or deleting irrecoverable personal files.
gaps.reason: No mechanism has been defined to prevent the software from deleting critical system files or user-sensitive documents.

gaps.impact: Significantly changes the tech stack choices and system APIs used (e.g. Win32 vs. POSIX).
gaps.reason: The specific target operating systems (Windows only vs. multi-platform) are undefined.

gaps.impact: Affects UI layout, page count, and scanning architecture.
gaps.reason: We do not know whether the user wants a simple, automated one-click cleanup or an advanced explorer of large files.

options.impact: Simpler API integration, faster development, and easier debugging.
options.label: Windows only for the MVP to prioritize speed and reliability.

options.impact: Broader target audience, but increases development and testing overhead.
options.label: Cross-platform support (Windows & macOS) right from the start.

questions.question: Which operating systems should the cleanup software support?
questions.reason: The target platform dictates the GUI framework and how we access system folders (like Temp, AppData, etc.).
questions.recommendation_reason: Since you are on Windows, starting with a Windows-focused app allows us to target specific system APIs and folders directly, reducing complexity before expanding.

options.impact: Very safe; allows users to recover files if needed, minimizing data loss risks.
options.label: Move files to Recycle Bin / Trash and apply a strict system directory whitelist.

options.impact: Recovers space instantly, but any accidental deletion is permanent and catastrophic.
options.label: Permanently delete files directly for maximum space recovery.

questions.question: How should the app handle file deletion to ensure user safety?
questions.reason: Deleting the wrong files can corrupt the operating system or delete precious user data, leading to severe complaints or data loss.
questions.recommendation: (Recommended) Send files to the Recycle Bin and use a strict whitelist.
questions.recommendation_reason: Moving files to the Recycle Bin provides an easy safety net for users to restore files, and a strict system-path whitelist prevents the app from touching crucial Windows files.

options.impact: Standard, clean user experience; easy to implement and understand.
options.label: Simple dashboard UI (Scan & Clean) with checkboxes for file categories.

options.impact: Excellent for manually finding space-hogging folders, but more complex to build.
options.label: Visual disk analyzer (like WinDirStat) showing directory tree maps.

questions.question: What UI layout and core user flow would you prefer?
questions.reason: The user experience determines whether we build a simple dashboard or an interactive disk explorer.
questions.recommendation: (Recommended) Dashboard with a simple 'Scan' and 'Clean' flow, plus category checkboxes.
questions.recommendation_reason: This is intuitive for all users, letting them see what categories (temp files, browser cache, etc.) are being cleaned without overwhelming them.

options.impact: Tiny application size, high performance, and modern web UI styling.
options.label: Tauri (Rust + Web frontend) for a lightweight, secure app.

options.impact: Easy to write and prototype, but results in a larger packaged file (~50-100MB).
options.label: Python (PySide/PyQt) for fast development and rich GUI library.

options.impact: Deep integration with Windows APIs and native performance, but Windows-locked.
options.label: C# (WPF) for native Windows-only integration.

questions.question: Do you have a preferred technology stack for the desktop application?
questions.reason: The choice of framework impacts build size, UI performance, and ease of packaging/distribution.
questions.recommendation_reason: Tauri produces extremely lightweight executable files (~5MB compared to Electron's ~100MB) and offers high performance and strong security.

risks: Data Loss: Accidental deletion of critical system files, active user files, or browser/app credentials.
System Instability: Cleaning system caches or registry entries can lead to operating system failures or application crashes.
Privilege Elevation: Scanning and deleting files in certain directories requires administrator rights, raising security concerns.
Performance degradation: Inefficient scanning of huge drives can consume 100% CPU/Disk I/O, freezing the computer.
unknowns: The specific operating systems to support (Windows only vs. cross-platform).
The preferred GUI design style (minimalist automated vs. power-user detailed control).
The deletion mechanism (direct deletion vs. recycling bin recycle vs. backup-before-deletion).
The technology stack preference (Tauri, Python, C#, Electron).
